ABOUT THIS HANDBOOK

This handbook is an introduction to MAS for new Volunteer Consultants (VCs) and a reference for current VCs. It does not replace ongoing participation for up-to-date information about MAS and how we operate.

MAS processes continue to change over time as we find better ways to operate and to serve non-profit clients.  This handbook captures our current organization and processes; it will be revised from time to time.  

This handbook reviews how MAS does business.  It does not attempt to teach VCs how to be effective consultants.  

You can always get up-to-date information from:

Nina Rahenbrock, Client Services Manager 	416-963-5792	info@masadvise.org

Paddy Bowen, Executive Director		647-633-9632 paddybowen59@gmail.com

Scott Russell, Board Chair					scott@russell.to

ABOUT MAS

Our Mission

MAS helps Not for Profit organizations and sub-sectors to develop and grow, especially those most in need, through the targeted use of MAS capabilities and expertise.

Our Vision

A strong and vibrant Not for Profit sector supported and equipped to create a more inclusive, equitable and just Canadian society.

Our Values  

Commitment to Clients

We are passionately committed to the success of our clients and their communities.  We act as trusted advisors and use all of our available resources to assist with the best possible solutions.

Volunteerism

We are committed to providing skilled volunteers with opportunities to give back to the communities we serve.  

Social Equity

We are committed to;

being a diverse, equitable and inclusive organization; our members represent the communities we serve

supporting all organizations working towards social equity and an end to systemic racism  

eliminating discrimination on any basis within MAS and assisting our clients in their efforts to do the same.

Continuous Learning

We believe that lifelong learning is essential for our volunteers to be able to deliver relevant, meaningful support to clients.  Through continuous learning we will continue to evolve our service offerings to best meet the needs of the sector.  

Systemic Change 

Through networking and partnerships, we will leverage our collective knowledge and experience to benefit the wider Not for Profit sector.

Our Strategy

In 2021 the MAS board updated our strategy for the next 5 years.  We will fund our operations through donations from clients, Volunteer Consultants and friends.  Our 5 key areas of strategic focus are:

MAS is a charitable organization.   We are an unparalleled source of no-fee consulting help for non-profit clients in the Greater Toronto Area. 

Our History

MAS was formed in 1993 by a few volunteers with a good idea.  The initial Volunteer Consultants came largely from the CESO (Canadian Executive Service Organization) roster of volunteers.  MAS was associated with the Volunteer Center of Toronto until 2004 when it became an independent corporation. 

In 2005 MAS was granted charitable status. In 2007, after a transition period, all VCs were invited to become members of MAS and a 10 member Board was elected.  

In 2008, the Board established an Executive Director position, filled by three volunteers (Sue Croft, Steve Gittins, and Sue Pulfer).  In 2022 our first paid (part time) Executive Director was hired, Paddy Bowen.

In 2009 we received a grant from Trillium to allow us to pay someone to administer the office, a part time Program Co-coordinator.  Nina Rahenbrock currently provides this service. 

In 2018 MAS celebrated its 25th year of offering pro bono services to charities and not for profits.  We have continued to increase the number of projects our Volunteer Consultants undertake for clients – for example in 2019 we received over 191 consulting assignments. 

What We Do

MAS attracts volunteers with extensive business/professional experience to provide management consulting services to non-profit clients.  Non-profit status is the only qualification we have for clients subject to them having the ability to take advantage of consulting assistance. We match our clients to skilled professional Volunteer Consultants. Services are delivered primarily to clients in the GTA however we may seek to expand our geographic area in future. 

MAS VCs must have the relevant skills and experience and an ability to forge strong relationships. At the core of the client relationships is trust.  A VC must build trust with the client, get a clear understanding of the client’s situation, and assist the client in identifying solutions they can implement.

Consultants undertake consulting assignments with specific deliverables.  VCs form a variety of relationships with their clients. Some consultants form longer-term relationships with clients and provide ongoing coaching or ad hoc consulting services (also defined projects).   VCs are encouraged to keep in touch with previous clients and to solicit further projects for MAS.

We have defined our consulting practices as below, to best match VCs to clients. However, if a client requests assistance that falls outside a practice area we will refer them to the most appropriate VC, if they have the expertise to do the assignment - whether or not it fits neatly in our categories.

MAS Consulting Practice areas

Governance

Strategic Planning

Human Resources, including volunteer management and coaching

Communications, Marketing and Fundraising

Information Management and Technology

Finance

New organization start-up

Exceptions

There are a few areas where MAS will decline to provide services.  We do not provide:

any service that requires a licensed professional (audit, legal advice, etc.)  

hands-on IT support (although we do IT consulting)

temporary employees or fill interim positions.

With these exceptions, we try our best to meet any request for consulting services keeping the MAS Mission always in mind:  MAS helps Not for Profit organizations and sub-sectors to develop and grow, especially those most in need, through the targeted use of MAS capabilities and expertise.

How We Do It

Marketing

MAS has a volunteer Marketing Team that builds our brand and markets our services to the sector.  This team ensures we have an active online presence and executes a broader marketing plan.  However, most of our business is from referrals or from previous clients.  VCs are encouraged to promote MAS services whenever opportunities arise.

Project Life Cycle (Appendix A)

Our basic project management process involves three forms that capture the agreement with the client at each stage of the project: 

Client Engagement 

Project Execution

Project Close 

Client Engagement (see Request for Consulting Services form p.9 )

Projects generally originate when a non-profit makes contact with the MAS office or with a VC they know or have been referred to by an outside party (e.g. a previous client).  Clients can contact the office via phone, email, website or regular mail.  The office responds to all enquiries, gathers initial information and asks the client to complete the Request for Consulting Services form.  

Once the request is fleshed out with all available information it is circulated by email to the group of VCs that are assigned to the practice area best suited to deal with it. VCs may then indicate an interest by notifying the MAS office.  The MAS office then puts the client and VC in touch with one another.  

If the request is unclear or there are many issues, the Client Services Manager will clarify over the telephone or, if necessary, arrange for one of our Generalists or Practice Leaders to contact the client and develop a request that is then circulated to the VCs in the relevant practice. 

The form makes clear that a volunteer consultant identified by MAS will be referred to the client. It also seeks client agreement that MAS will not be liable for any loss or damage incurred by the Organization or third parties affected by or involved in the Project as a result of the consulting/advisory services provided by the volunteer consultant referred to the Organization by MAS.

Project Execution (see Project Definition form p.9 )

When the VC accepts an assignment, the VC meets with the client, establishes a relationship and develops a Project Definition that defines the deliverables and is signed by the client and the VC.  

It is very important to the success of a project that the VC clarifies the client’s expectations, that the client and the VC understand their respective roles in the project and that the deliverables are clear. If for any reason the VC or Client decides not to proceed then the MAS office should be advised and, if called for, another VC will be assigned. 

At this stage it is important to explain to the client, especially new clients, who MAS is and how we operate, including the fact that we are financed largely by client donations and that the organization will ask the client to consider a donation at the close of the project. (This “ask” may be done by the Volunteer Consultant or by the Executive Director).  However, whether or not a client makes a donation has no impact on our response to future requests for service.

Most projects occur through a series of meetings over a couple of months.  Sometimes there are significant delays in the work due to client capacity or timing and on occasion projects can be protracted. In these cases, the VC is responsible for ensuring that the client still feels there is a priority for the project. If the client is not able to support the project, it can be put on hold until the client can support it. Projects should not be put on hold for longer than 6 months. When a project has been on hold for 6 months the client services manager will review the project with the VC to see if it should be closed, cancelled or left on hold.  If necessary, the project can be cancelled.

The deliverables and how they are accomplished vary by the type of assignment.  Meetings may take place at the client’s place of business, by telephone or by videoconference and the VC also does work at home (e.g., meeting preparation, documentation, report writing).  A VC may work alone or ask for help from other VCs. VCs are encouraged to work together, as appropriate. This promotes learning and development as well as shares the workload.

Generally, we undertake only one project at a time for a client.  Most of our clients are small and cannot handle multiple projects simultaneously.  In cases involving several issues (e.g. governance, financial management, planning) we will work with the client to establish a priority and do one project at a time. However, if we do agree to a second project while another is still open a Project Definition will be required for the second project but not an RCS.

Project Close  

When the project has been completed the VC has a discussion with the client to review the original Project Definition and discuss the work completed and outcomes delivered.  This is an excellent time to ask for feedback from the client; 

what went well

what did we learn

are there opportunities for future projects between MAS and the client

IF comfortable and it seems appropriate, mention the possibility of a donation (NOTE: the MAS office will include this ask in closing documentation as well)

     The VC advises the client that they will be receiving a Project Close email from MAS and  

     requests that they complete the information and return to MAS.

      Many VCs follow up this final conversation with a “thank you” email.

Client Meetings

Client meetings may take place in person, by phone or by video conference.  MAS has a Zoom account that all VCs are welcome to use.  To book a Zoom meeting, email the Client Services Manager (info@masadvise.org) and provide the date and time of your meeting.  The Client Services Manager will send you an email confirming your reservation with the details.

MAS FORMS

All current forms are posted in the VC Reference Library on the internal web page www.masadvise.org/vcs  

Request for Consulting Services [RCS]

This is the basic consulting agreement. It should be completed by a new client prior to any service provision and sent to the MAS office.  If we have dealt with the client previously and have a fairly recent (2 years) form on file, it is not necessary to complete another one though often they do which helps define the current project.

If the client contact person has changed then the original RCS should be shared with the new client contact.

Project Definition

This is the agreement between the VC and the client on the specific deliverables for the project. It should be completed at the start of the project with the client and sent to the MAS office.

Reporting: Monthly Status Reports

Each month the VC is required to provide a brief (sentence or two) update on activities in the past month and expected activities in the next month for every open project.  The Client Services Manager will email the VCs a link to a web form used to provide these updates.  This information is critical to managing the active projects.

Project Close

When the work has been completed, the VC completes a Project Close form.  The form is forwarded to the MAS office who then forwards it to the client. The client is invited to add their comments to the Project Close form and return to the MAS office, however, this is not required. 

The following are detailed instructions on how to complete the Project Close form:

Please add this link to your favourites in your browser:	

https://masadvise.org/mas-project-close-form/

All of the information gathered is extremely important for MAS, including:

Hours worked on the project

Benefits gained by the client

Client comments on their level of satisfaction and willingness to work with MAS again

The client’s approval to use their quotes in MAS Social Media posts

An optional referral from the client to another organization

Without the Project Close form, it is very difficult to track project quality, the impact of our work, total hours contributed to MAS clients, create content for our Social Media etc.

VC - Instructions for completing the form

There are two parts to the online form – one for the VC and one for the client.

Click on your saved link (see above) to go to the project close page on the MAS website

Click on the link to open the form

Fill in all the fields in the top section (called the Volunteer Consultant section)

Scroll down past the Client section to the bottom of the form and click on “VC save and continue later”

You will be given a link. Right click and copy the link to your clipboard.

Draft and send an email to the Client Services Manager (info@masadvise.org) requesting that she closes the project. Paste the link (from your clipboard) into the email.

What happens then...

The Client Services Manager sends the link to the client with a personalized note asking them to complete the MAS Project Close form using the link and thanking them for working with MAS etc.  The Client Services Manager will then close the project in the database.

The client clicks the link and fills out the client portion of the form and clicks on the “submit” button to submit it.

The completed form will then reside on our WordPress database allowing the Client Services Manager to access it and run reports.

If you feel it is inappropriate to ask the client to fill in the client portion (project cancelled, ED resigned etc.), then complete the VC portion and send the link to the Client Services Manager telling her the reason. They will put the reason in the client portion and submit it when they close the project. 

When a project closes, the VC may choose to encourage the client to consider a donation to MAS but there is no requirement to do so.  The MAS office will ask for a donation during the administrative closing process.  In our experience most clients will willingly make a contribution if they have the funds.  Our story as a volunteer organization with minimal expenses supported largely by our volunteers and our clients is a powerful one. 

Notes:

The Project Close form captures the hours spent by VCs on a project.  VCs must track these hours.  If more than one VC is involved in the project then hours for each VC should be recorded. This information is critical to MAS in making our case about the value we provide to the community.

These forms are the required paperwork for every project undertaken by MAS.  The forms must be sent to the MAS office promptly.  Every VC should be familiar with these forms. As the forms are revised from time to time new versions are posted to the VC Support Centre on the internal web page. 

If the Volunteer Consultant has elected to ask the client for a donation they must alert the Client Services Manager so we don’t duplicate the request unknowingly during the closing process.

Donations from Clients

Donations from our clients have grown steadily over the last few years and we need to ensure this continues. VCs play an important part in this. The fact that we accept donations is displayed prominently on all standard MAS forms that our clients review, plus on all our promotional material. Therefore, they know we are looking for donations. 

In the initial meeting with a client the VC should inform them that, while we do not charge fees, we do accept donations to cover our office expenses. 

At the end of the project, the subject of donations will again be raised. As noted above this may be done by the VC if it makes sense and/or a request for a donation will be made by the Executive Director as part of the closing process.

An example of what might be inserted in that email is as follows:

“As you know, MAS is financially supported by our volunteers and donations from our clients. If you were satisfied with the results of this assignment, we would appreciate it if you would consider a donation to help us keep the office running”

In the instance where a VC raises the possibility of a donation with the client, the Client Services Manager and/or ED should be alerted so the ‘request for a donation’ letter can be adjusted accordingly.

How much to ask for

You may be asked to suggest the size of a donation. The following notes, expressed in your own words, are what you might say in response to such a request.

“MAS receives a wide range of donations mostly from $100 to $1,000 with an average of about $500 and with some as high as $5,000.  Organizations usually set the amount in keeping with their budget and the consulting time spent on the project and their degree of satisfaction with the outcomes.” 


Obviously, many agencies cannot afford to donate and in that case we don’t expect any donation at all.

Our Volunteer Consultants

MAS has a proud history of attracting Volunteer Consultants who have provided great value to the non-profit sector in the GTA.  

The following is the Board policy on Volunteer Management: 

“MAS provides consulting services to non-profits.  We recruit experienced individuals with a range of skills and backgrounds to provide these services.  Our volunteer management processes are transparent and designed to ensure MAS consultants provide value to clients and that we have internal volunteers to assist the Client Services Manager in conducting MAS activities.  Volunteers are invited to be members of MAS, but membership is not a requirement.

The ED has overall responsibility for attracting volunteers to MAS.  They must ensure that the appropriate processes and structures are in place so that MAS has a sufficient roster of qualified Volunteer Consultants.

MAS will attract Volunteer Consultants based on project volumes and required expertise.

Volunteer Consultant candidates will be interviewed by a Practice Leader and will have a follow up discussion and orientation with the Executive Director.

If a volunteer is working on internal MAS projects, it is the responsibility of the Executive Director to ensure appropriate management and oversight.

All volunteers must qualify for volunteer positions/roles according to the qualification process for specific positions/roles as specified and monitored by the Executive Director from time to time.

Each volunteer role/position will have a job description in place.

All volunteers must sign a Code of Conduct agreement.”

VC Role Description -  Appendix B

Our consultants have a broad range of business/professional experience, in-depth knowledge and skills and want to make a difference in the community.  Many are retirees, some have their own businesses, and some are employed full-time.  MAS expects VCs to contribute at least 40 hours per year which broadly translates to about 2 assignments but could be more.

MAS Code of Conduct (Appendix D)

Each VC must sign the MAS Code of Conduct when they join MAS.  It covers conflict of interest issues, expenses, confidentiality, privacy and MAS reputation.  

MAS Confidentiality Policy (Appendix E)

MAS Sexual Harassment, Anti-Oppression and Anti-Racism Policy (Appendix E)

Volunteer Consultant Bios and Photos

All VCs will be asked to provide a photograph and bio which will be posted to the MAS internal website.

How Projects are Assigned

When a new VC joins MAS, they are assigned to specific practice areas (e.g. facilitation, finance, strategic planning).  The normal process is for new client requests to be circulated via email to the VCs in the relevant practice and each of those VCs has the opportunity to accept the assignment. 

Our Structure

MAS is an incorporated entity and has charitable status.  We are a membership corporation with an elected Board of Directors.  The organization chart and contact information is attached as Appendix G.

MAS members may attend the Annual General Meeting and vote on matters affecting the corporation, including election of Board members. All VCs are encouraged to become members and take part in the corporate business, but corporate membership is not a requirement.  Currently, anyone who makes at least a $50 donation to MAS and is approved by the Board is made a member through to the following AGM. 

The Executive Director role is responsible to the Board for the operations and management of MAS.  A paid part time individual currently fills this role which until 2022 was carried out by volunteers. Other volunteers fill additional roles in the management structure (see organization chart) and provide assistance in the office and work on special projects from time to time.

The Client Services Manager (CSM) is responsible for the office and is the primary initial client contact as well as the point of coordination for most routine activities e.g. receiving and dealing with client requests or consulting assistance.  

We encourage VCs to become involved in ongoing MAS work. This is an excellent way to get to know the organization, the sector and other VCs.  To volunteer for any of these areas, contact the appropriate person on the organization chart.

Financial Matters

MAS operates on a very limited budget.  Our main expense is the services of the Client Services Manager and the Executive Director which are both part time positions. Our principal funding sources are clients and our VCs and our policy is to operate as a financially self-sufficient organization, supported by agencies who benefit from our service and VC donations.

Resources

It is important for all VCs to get an understanding of the non-profit sector and the broad issues and trends impacting it.  In addition, it is useful to develop an understanding of issues affecting specific sub-sectors (e.g. newcomer services, senior services, environmental, arts, etc.).  This expertise develops over time but there are many useful sources of information, including your Practice Leader and fellow VCs.  Our current Executive Director is a very experienced nfp sector executive as well and can be a very helpful resource to VC’s as well

Appendix E - MAS Confidentiality Policy

Background

The purpose of this policy is to ensure that all individuals working on behalf of MAS, all volunteer consultants, all Internal Volunteers, MAS contract workers, and any Director acting in his/her capacity as a member of the Board of Directors of MAS, working with organizations to whom they are referred by MAS (“MAS Organizations”), understand and agree with the importance of protecting from unauthorized disclosure all confidential information made available to them by MAS and/or MAS Organizations to whom they are referred both during periods of volunteer engagement and after completion of such engagements. This policy is intended to safeguard the integrity and reputations of MAS and MAS Organizations.

Policy Statement

MAS seeks to secure and protect from unauthorized disclosure all information related to MAS including its organization, strategies, business plans and operation and the information made available to MAS by MAS Organizations to whom referrals are made of volunteer consultants.

Each volunteer consultant who has agreed to act in such capacity with a MAS Organization to whom he/she is referred following an assessment of a Request for Consulting Services, and any MAS contract worker or internal volunteer or Director who has access to MAS Organization Confidential Information, must agree to the terms of this Policy by signing the MAS Code of Conduct prior to doing any work for MAS requiring their need to access any MAS Organization information.

Confidential Information for the purposes of this policy shall include:

Technical data, research, products, financial information, plans or strategies, forecasts or forecast assumptions, business practices, operations, procedures or services or marketing, merchandising or pricing information whether in documentary or electronic form;

Personal information about any individual;

Proprietary information of a Client Organization;	or

Any information that is designated or labeled as “Confidential” by MAS or a Client Organization that is given to or made accessible to MAS or a volunteer consultant who has been referred to the Client Organization by MAS.

By signing the MAS Code of Conduct, the signatory agrees:

to use the same reasonable precautions they would use to protect the confidential and proprietary information of their own or their clients, if any, in order to maintain the secrecy and confidentiality of such information;

not to disclose any Confidential Information to a third party (except as required by law) without the prior written consent of the disclosing party;

not to use the Confidential Information for any purpose other than as required to carry out any assignments resulting from referrals by MAS which the volunteer consultant has agreed to with the MAS Organization that the latter has disclosed to the volunteer consultant or MAS;

only to disclose the Confidential Information to MAS or other volunteer consultants or internal volunteers or third parties which MAS or the MAS Organization, as the case may be, agrees have a need to know the Confidential Information and who have signed a MAS Code of Conduct as well; and

not to make copies of Confidential information except as may be required for the performance of assignments with MAS Organizations to whom the volunteer consultant has been referred, or in the case of MAS contract workers, internal volunteers or Directors, who have a need to know the Confidential Information of such MAS Organization. All copies will upon reproduction contain the same proprietary and confidential notices and legends, which appear on the original documents and information

The obligations of confidentiality set out in this Policy do not apply to information that:

must be disclosed by law, judicial or arbitration process or by government authorities provided that the party required to disclose first gives the other party reasonable notice of such law, order or process;

is disclosed by the receiving party with prior written consent of the disclosing party; or

is otherwise in the public domain through no fault of the receiving party.

The receiving party, upon request of the disclosing party, agrees to return all Confidential Information to the disclosing party or destroy such Confidential Information and copies, if any, as directed by the disclosing party.

If the receiving party discovers that it has lost any Confidential Information it shall immediately notify the disclosing party.

Appendix F - MAS Sexual Harassment, Anti-Oppression and Anti-Racism Policy

Background

MAS is committed to providing an environment that is inclusive, equitable and free of discrimination and harassment, in which all volunteers are treated with respect and dignity, are able to contribute fully, and have equal opportunities.

Policy

Under the Ontario Human Rights Code, every person has the right to freedom from harassment and discrimination. Harassment and discrimination will not be tolerated, condoned, or ignored at MAS. If a claim of harassment or discrimination is proven, disciplinary measures will be applied, up to and including termination of a volunteer’s relationship with MAS. 

MAS is committed to making its volunteers aware of its anti-harassment and anti- discrimination policies. 

The objectives of this Policy are to:

Ensure that volunteers are aware that harassment and discrimination are unacceptable practices and are incompatible with the standards of the organization, as well as being a violation of the law.

Set out the types of behaviour that may be considered offensive and are prohibited by this Policy.

The right to freedom from discrimination and harassment extends to all volunteers, casual helpers and contract staff.

It is also unacceptable for any of the above to engage in harassment or discrimination when dealing with MAS clients, or with others with whom they have professional dealings, such as suppliers or service providers. Behaviours prohibited by this policy include discrimination, harassment, sexual harassment, sexual solicitation and poisoning of the environment. 

This Policy applies to every aspect of the workplace environment including volunteer recruitment and selection. This Policy also applies to events that occur with MAS clients.

This Policy prohibits discrimination or harassment on the basis of the following grounds, and any combination of these grounds:

Age

Creed (religion)

Sex (including pregnancy and breastfeeding)

Gender Identity

Family status (such as being in a parent-child relationship)

Marital status (including the status of being married, single, widowed, divorced, separated, or living in a conjugal relationship outside of marriage, whether in a same sex or opposite sex relationship)

Disability (including mental, physical, developmental or learning disabilities)

Race

Ancestry

Place of origin

Ethnic origin

Citizenship

Colour

Record of offences includes provincial offences such as under the Highway Traffic Act, and federal offences for which a pardon has been granted. 

All persons present in MAS are expected to uphold and abide by this Policy, by refraining from any form of harassment or discrimination, and by cooperating fully in any investigation of a harassment or discrimination complaint.

MAS leadership have the additional responsibility to act immediately on complaints or observations of harassment or discrimination. All complaints will be dealt with in a confidential manner respecting all parties involved. Leaders are responsible for creating and maintaining a harassment and discrimination-free organization, and should address potential problems before they become serious.

title: Virtual Consulting - Using Zoom Whiteboard
content:
# Virtual Consulting - Using Zoom Whiteboard

Source: VC Support Centre (Google Drive)

MAS Strategic Planning

Using the new Zoom Whiteboard to facilitate Zoom brainstorming sessions

As a MAS Strategic Planning consultant, I struggled early in the pandemic (as did we all) to transfer the brainstorming techniques learned and honed in live sessions with client boards and management to something we could use in a virtual session. Developing a solid strategic plan always had involved getting everyone in a room, soliciting their ideas about the future and working as a team to determine the key themes identified, leading to the strategies and finally a strategic plan. 

Live Brainstorming

When the pandemic took hold and we all realized that we needed to find a solution that did not involve being in a room together, we all scrambled to find out what tools were out there and how best to make use of them. Now, despite the pandemic having passed for the most part, many clients have decided that the convenience of Zoom is something they would like to continue using. Those who live in the GTA love not having to drive in rush-hour traffic to join a board meeting. Organizations that are national appreciate involving all members of the team instead of just those that are local or that can afford to fly in for a brainstorming session. 

Tools like MIRO or the older version of the Zoom Whiteboard (with little to no functionality) seemed to hamper the experience of brainstorming on Zoom rather than enhance it. Instead, Zoom meetings were held with the working groups, ideas were discussed and shared, some amount of grouping of ideas and working on key themes was done in breakout sessions, eventually leading to an end product. 

The NEW Zoom Whiteboard

Features released by Zoom late in 2022 provide a much more user-friendly, and simple to use whiteboard functionality. The templates provided are very simple to copy and use. The setup of groupings and easily-updated and moveable yellow stickies is simple to use live with clients or preparing a whiteboard prior to a Zoom call.

Example of Brainstorming technique

After a bit of trial and error what I have found to be most useful for myself and my clients it to have them do some “homework” or pre-work prior to the Zoom session, sending me information which I then use to pre-populate the brainstorming whiteboard. Think of this as replacing the time in the live session where you ask each client for 5 ideas about, for instance, what the ideal ABC organization should look like 5 years from now and they fill out their 5 ideas on 5 yellow stickies. This visioning session is usually the first team brainstorming session I do with clients. 

The members of the strategic planning working team are asked to email me their “5 yellow stickies” containing their 5 ideas of what the org should ideally look like 5 years from now. After receiving an email from all team members with bullet-point suggestions, I then open a Zoom Whiteboard. This doesn’t need to be done in a live Zoom session and, in fact, works best if done prior to a live session. I fill in the whiteboard with the ideas sent by the team. I take a first pass at grouping the stickies into themes or groupings to come up with a draft whiteboard. Think of this as replacing the time in a live session where you, the facilitator, sometimes with help from a working team member, put the yellow-stickies on the board and attempt to group them into themes.

To do this, I open the Zoom Whiteboard, copy the simplest template, cut and paste to add groupings and stickies, fill in the wording in each yellow-sticky and group the stickies into my themes or groupings. You can then use the Export option in the menu to export the draft Whiteboard to PDF.

The next step is to send the draft whiteboard to working team members and ask them to review it prior to the Zoom session. It will look something like this:

Live Zoom Brainstorming session

Now that you’ve collected the team’s ideas and drafted the first cut of the whiteboard, it’s time for a live Zoom session. The members should be coming to the Zoom having reviewed the draft whiteboard, preparing any questions or suggestions they might have for updating and improving it. Once the live session begins I usually start by summarizing the steps we’ve taken so far in our strategic planning efforts be they surveys, focus groups, environmental scans etc. Then I remind them that the process we are taking replaces the steps we would usually have done together in a room in a live brainstorming session (collecting their ideas on yellow stickies, posting and grouping them on the wall) and we are now ready to review what we’ve created and see how we might change it, update, add, reword, and move things around.

Typically, I work through the Whiteboard one grouping at a time, reading out the yellow-stickies for that particular theme and then asking if anyone has any questions about the content.  Some team members will want clarification about certain yellow-stickies, others can provide their input. Once questions are answered we move to the next grouping. Once all groupings are completed, I ask if there are any key things we feel are missing. Members will suggest ideas and I create a new yellow-stickie by cutting and pasting (right click) any of the yellow-stickies and changing the wording the what is suggested by the team member, moving it around as needed. Finally, if there is debate about a stickie fitting better in one grouping than another, the stickies can be moved around. 

What you end up with is very similar to what you would have up on the wall in a live session. In a live session I used to take a picture of what was on the wall with my iPad, facilitating the documentation of the session after the fact as well as providing photos of the team’s work which I shared with the team in the post-brainstorming write-up. 

You can now proceed as you would in a live session. I like to ask if these things are doable and have impact, using the concept of the do-ability/impact grid (Highly doable and high impact in top right, hard to do and low impact in bottom left). You can do that as a grid using a separate whiteboard or just talk it through taking notes. Using whatever techniques you like to close it out, you now have completed a productive brainstorming session where all members feel like they’ve had their “say” and have saved a lot of time (rather than having to let each member speak on the Zoom) of the typical brainstorming Zoom session.

title: MAS Annotated Resource List
content:
# MAS Annotated Resource List

Source: MAS Resource Library (SharePoint)

MAS Annotated Resource List for Volunteer Consultants

June 2023

Over the years volunteers working with MAS have compiled an excellent set of on-line tools, articles and other resources in our MAS Resource Library.  They have been organized mostly along the Practice areas of MAS: governance, strategic planning, finance, fundraising etc.

Because by this point there are so many resources and because a quick look into the many Libraries and Folders doesn’t really tell you what’s in there without having to open each item, we have decided to put together this listing of titles with VERY brief descriptions.  

Although VCs are organized into Practice areas you may find helpful resources for your various projects in other areas; we’d recommend you scan this whole listing as there may be resources in different Libraries that can help you (or your client).

What’s great about the MAS Resource Library is that our VCs have done an amazing job of curating a wide range of items.  In future if and when you discover helpful tools, information, articles etc. it would be great if you could send us a copy so we can upload it. This slightly veers away from the previous process where any VC could insert a document directly.  

Moving forward we will continue to track new resources as they come in and maintain this annotated list.  The list itself will be kept on the VC page of the website and of course be available to send out on request.  We also often get requests from people needing various kinds of help or  information about not-for-profit life.  Now being able to put our hand quickly onto a resource we can share will be invaluable to our ability to respond.

If you have any comments or questions please don’t hesitate to contact me, or Nina (Client Services Manager).

Paddy Bowen, Executive Director, MAS

647-633-9632

Paddybowen59@gmail.com

Strategic Planning 

Articles and Papers

Are You Doing the SWOT Analysis Backwards? by Laurence Minsky and David Aron,  2021

Interesting article from the Harvard Business Review.

Roles in Strategic Planning

Quick 2-page rundown of roles of Board, consultant, staff etc.

Charting a New Path Forward, Boardsource, 2017

A piece produced by Boardsource when they engaged in their own Strategic Planning process; includes six “Insights” that are interesting to ponder.

Two Signs that Your Strategy Needs a Refresh, Meera Chary, 2018

4-page discussion on when/why a new SP could be called for.

How to Brainstorm — Remotely, by Art Markman, 2020

From the Harvard Business Review – very helpful think piece on some of the challenges – and benefits – of working remotely.

FACILITATING REMOTE WORKSHOPS; THE DEFINITIVE GUIDE TO Insights, tools, and case studies from digital-first companies and expert facilitator

Very detailed (76 pages) document filled with discussion, strategies, tips and guides for working remotely as a leader or facilitator.

The Best Time to Say Yes: How Strategic Planning Can Help, Bridgespan Group Vlad Nedelea July 29, 2019 

Two-page think piece on reasons to embark of SP.

Strategic Thinking: How to Do Strategic Planning Like a Futurist, by Amy Webb, 2019

An argument for longer-term strategic planning i.e. a ten year ‘vista’…

Making Strategic Planning (Relatively) Painless, by Tanya Ishikawa, 2021

Six “quick tips” for SP.

Market Research for Strategic Planning T. Hodapp 2018

Great little 2-page guide written for MAS by one of our Marketing Practice VC’s.

Merging Nonprofit Organizations: The Art and Science of the Deal by John A. Yankey, Ph.D. Barbara Wester Jacobus, M. N. O., Kelly McNally Koney, M. S. S. A., 2001

Although this is an older book it’s an exhaustive analysis of everything you’d need to think about before and during an NFP merger process.

Ontario Nonprofit Network Shared Platform Guide, 2016

This guidebook provides good practices, for the implementation of shared platforms. “The shared platform approach supports collaboration, leadership, governance and project development for a diverse range of sector-specific work, neighbourhood work, networks and time-limited initiatives. The approach fosters social innovation, providing the opportunity for experimentation and the testing of new ideas”.

Strategic Planning Amidst Uncertainty, The Bridgespan Group, 2021

Power point format – great overview of questions you might pose to a Board before embarking on an SP.

What It Takes to Run a Great Virtual Meeting, by Bob Frisch and Cary Greene, 2020

Good little tips documents – basic but helpful.

How Nonprofits and NGOs Can Get Real Value from Strategic Planning, The Bridgespan Group, 2023

Excellent article at the Bridgespan Group website.  They are a global company that provide consulting help and guidance to NGO's.  The article found by clicking this link covers the following:

"Strategic planning is about making decisions that provide clarity and alignment to best put critical resources to use to achieve your nonprofit's goals. It sounds simple, yet many organizations struggle with the process, not knowing why, where, or how to start. This article can help. It shares four vital elements common to most strategic planning approaches and a number of common pitfalls to avoid."
By: Lindsey Waldron, Preeta Nayak, Teni Lanre-Amos, Bradley Seeman, for Bridgespan, June 2023

Tools and Templates

 Strategic Planning Key Questions to Ask

A very helpful little guide to the homework you can do as a VC BEFORE you start off on a Strategic Planning process with an NFP.  Written by MAS VC Sue Pulfer, 2014.

Strategic Plan Template

Easy to copy little format that shows how you might lay out a goal, beside indicators of success.  Developed by MAS VC Chris Govern.

Strategic & Action Planning Steps

A 3-point summary developed by Dorothy Aaron, VC, in 2014.

Strategic Planning Process Template

Developed by Chris Govern (2014): “I use this when talking to a client about strategic planning.  I customize to the steps we agree to, add dates, etc.   I find this is a useful way to make sure we all know what we need to do by when.  I can update this as plans change.”

KEY INFORMANT QUESTIONS RE: STRATEGIC PLANNING

Six questions you may choose to address to “key informants” external to the organization doing a Strategic Plan.

Environmental Scan Template Small Organization

Nice little guide providing the questions you can use while doing an environmental scan with a smaller NFP.

SHORT TERM SCENARIO PLANNING SAMPLE (FRAMEWORK)

Very helpful template showing how an NFP might work through different future scenarios by topic, based on 3 possible futures i.e. optimistic, most likely, pessimistic.

Sample SWOT and Survey Results prepared by S Pulfer 2017

Excellent example of a SWOT report back to an organization (this is based on a real case but made anonymous here).

Sample Operational Plan template (Sue Pulfer, 2018)

Easy to adapt model of how an annual operational plan can be laid out.

Sample Strategic Plan – S Pulfer/2017

Easy to use format – six goals over four years – this document is an example of a one-year plan of action against the goals.

Sample of a visual depiction (chart) of a five-year strategic plan

Operational Plan Template (Chris Govern, 2014)

Easy to cut and paste…

ICEBREAKER EXERCISE: Coat of Arms (Chris Govern developed)

Neat way to get a session going asking participants to work in small groups to create their organizations ‘coat of arms’.  Gets them thinking about goals and succinct descriptions etc.

Presentations and Workshops

Slide presentation on OGSM method of Strategic Planning

Use as both a guide for you, the VC and as a presentation to your client.  OGSM= 

Objectives - what we want to achieve, in words

Goals - what we want to achieve, in numbers

Strategies – the choices we make for how to achieve the objectives & goal

Measures – how to measure progress for each strategy (assess if working to achieve the goal)

What is Strategic Planning – deck

Simple overview (27 slides)

Introduction to Strategic Planning

Similar kind of overview (28 slides)

Essentials of Strategic Planning, by VC Mark Ellwood, 2018

Another overview presentation – bit longer at 40 slides

Governance

Editors Note:  The Governance Library has amassed a LOT of great resources.  As you’ll see there are four discrete folders (Articles, Workshops/Presentations, Templates/Tools and Incorporation Information).  Because the MAS libraries and folders have not been ‘managed’ in any way there are resources in one folder that could as easily be in another, depending on where the contributor of the resource put it.  For example, you might see workshop presentations in Articles and think pieces in Presentations etc.  For now, please scan the contents of all four folders when you’re looking for governance information.  A future project for us at MAS will be to move things around for more consistency.  Happy reading!

Articles and Papers

7 Ideas to Build a Healthy Board Nomination Process

Helpful resource to share with ED’s and Boards

360-degree Governance and Where are the Directors in a World in Crisis

A 55-page examination from a practical and scholarly standpoint what good governance in the 21st century should be.  Produced by the Rotman School and written by Peter Dey and Susan Kaplan and with input from a huge Advisory Committee of Canadian corporate Who’s Who.  It’s from a very corporate perspective so lots is not applicable to NFP’s, however the 13 principals outlined in the 360-degree governance model would be very interesting for any Board – including not-for-profit, to adopt.

2017 Social and Demographic Trends by Jim Russell

An interesting short (3 page) discussion that explores a variety of issues and poses a number of questions for NFP Leaders such as “Despite your best efforts to master and deal with the new world of social media, how else might your business model be challenged in the era of the disappearance of context and attention spans?”.  Could form the basis of an interesting Board discussion session.

Imagine Canada’s Standards Program for Canada’s Charities and Nonprofits

This resource touches on all areas of MAS work and provides the baseline standard of practice in five areas: A. board governance B. financial accountability & transparency C. fundraising D. staff management and E. volunteer involvement.  The Standards Program is first and foremost a capacity-building initiative and Imagine Canada encourage organizations to use the standards to improve and monitor their practices.  They also run a vigorous accreditation program based on the Standards but it is neither required or in fact used very much as there is no widespread expectation among funders, the public etc. that NFP’s should be accredited.

CCA (Canadian Centre for Accreditation) Standards Manual for Community- Based Primary Health Care Organizations, Edition Date: May 11, 2020

Another accreditation guide, the standards outlined in this manual have been grouped especially for the Community-Based Primary Health Care organizations. The Organizational Standards in Section 2 apply to all organizations. Section 3 is sector specific, such as community-based primary care, child and youth mental health or credit counselling. Contact CCA to ensure you are using the correct manual for your sector.

Peering into the Future: Reimagining Governance in the Non-Profit Sector, BY LISA LALANDE, funded by Ignite NPS.

This paper focuses on how non-profit organizations can adapt to an increasingly complex environment by reimagining governance. It addresses how boards, leaders, staff and key stakeholders can work together to contribute to effective organizational governance from a strategic perspective. Specifically, this paper will: » Explore the current state of governance in the sector, including the legislative, regulatory and policy environment. » Identify emerging trends and challenges that impact governance at both the organizational and sector level. » Discuss promising practices and key considerations to improve the current state of governance. » Provide recommendations to improve the sector’s capacity for “future-oriented governance.”

Slide presentation: “Beyond Boards: Reimagining Governance, Disrupting the Status Quo” by Erin Kang - Ontario Nonprofit Network and Linda Mollenhauer - Ignite NPS

Covers: Overview of the Reimagining Governance Initiative and results of some of their consultations.  The Reimagining Governance, convened by the Ontario Nonprofit Network in partnership with Ignite NPS who produced the paper (above).  Reimagining Governance is an initiative designed to spark dialogue and new approaches to the way that nonprofit organizations are governed.  This slide presentation provides a glimpse of some interesting alternative views on NFP governance but wouldn’t likely be something MAS VCs would use with clients – at this point.

Restoring Trust in Nonprofits, ONN, 2019

23-slide presentation with some interesting statistics and information.  Good to review if you’re interested in the topic of trust but otherwise not likely a tool many VCs would use.

Board Recruitment and Selection - Imagine Canada blog 2018

Short discussion by Suanne Miedema, President of Miedema’s Board Consulting Inc. where she helps nonprofit boards improve their governance.

BOARD RECRUITMENT MATRIX

This matrix can be adapted to assist an organization’s recruitment efforts by assessing current board composition and identifying opportunities to diversify and/or expand the board.

Guide to Good Governance: Not-for-Profit and Charitable Organizations, 2013.  

276-page guide produced by The Governance Centre of Excellence (GCE), an initiative of the Ontario Hospital Association.  An excellent “primer” on every topic related to governance you could think of.

Ontario NFP Update on new ONCA Legislation

With a note from VC Bill Sparks describing the content here: “A very comprehensive update from Carol Jackson on ONCA and the need for our VCs to advise caution before changing Provincial NFP corporations’ by-laws”.

MAS Governance Framework Issues and Elements

This is an excellent little resource to get you thinking about Boards from different perspectives.  It includes a very brief overview of various models of Board leadership (Carver, the Pragmatic Approach etc.) as well as “the four questions to be asked when you’re serving on a Board”.

Merging for Good: A Case-Based Framework for Supporting Effective Nonprofit Amalgamations

Written in 2021 after a pandemic induced merger of two NFP’s in Calgary.  This excellent 30 page report outlines the imperatives and challenges of nonprofit mergers and uses this case study to walk through the process.

20 Questions Directors of Not-for-Profit Organizations Should Ask about Mergers by Mark Blumberg • Andrea Cohen Barrack of CPAC (Chartered Professional Accountants of Canada)

Very thorough 56-page document: “Determining whether an organization should explore or proceed with a merger is one of the most important strategic and governance questions a board of directors can face. This document addresses the major elements directors should consider when contemplating a merger, grouped into the following areas:

 	1. Evaluating merger as a strategic option

2. Exploring a merger

3. Negotiating a merger

4. Implementing a merger”

Nine Lessons from a Nonprofit Advocacy Win, Posted by Danielle M. Henry on Boardsource, Jul 13, 2016

An informally written case study of a small local organization’s experience with an advocacy project.

Board Essentials, produced by the Ontario Nonprofit Network, 

This is an absolutely key document for general reference for any VC working with a Board.  A quick, 7-page, summary of the key responsibilities of a Board.  Could be used as a handout as well. 

“Board Essentials describes the requirements and responsibilities that must be fulfilled by the

board of directors, and which no other person or entity can perform. This core work of the board is based on what the law and regulations state are the requirements and responsibilities they must meet. While the board might play a significant role in fulfilling other governance functions, these are the essential ones.”  

Policy Statements (example) based on the Carver Board Governance Model

Produced by John Howard Society in 2014.  This is a helpful tool just to give you and idea of what a Board policy document, using the Carver Policy governance model, could look like.  For example, the short but easily used elsewhere Executive Limitation policy illustrates the Carver approach where the ED does everything, EXCEPT what the Board limitation policy explicitly states.

Pro’s and Con’s of Charitable Status

Great little (3 page) discussion piece by MAS VC Graham Boyce.

Top 10 Compliance Issues for Canadian Registered Charities. Presentation to the Sustainability Network, January 26, 2017, Mark Blumberg (mark@blumbergs.ca), Blumberg Segal LLP

Super helpful and clear 63-slide power point presentation, laying out exactly what the title indicates.  A must read for all Governance VC’s.

Voices of Board Chairs: A National Study on the Perspectives of Nonprofit Board Chairs, By Judy Freiwirth, Mary Hiland, Michael Burns, Gayle Gifford and Debra Beck | October 12, 2016

Very interesting discussion paper (17 pages).  An American perspective although that likely doesn’t change the perspective dramatically.  From the authors:  “As a group of practitioner researchers, we decided to find out what preparation is done by board chairs and how they see their role in relationship to the board and other stakeholders. What we found was a pretty glaring picture of neglect, in that this is an area of organizational leadership succession that is often insufficiently thought through. What follows are our findings from a survey of 635 self-identified nonprofit board chairs representing local, regional, and national organizations in forty-two states, and the recommendations to nonprofits we make in light of these findings.”

The Effective Board Manual: The Manual as an Orientation Tool and Guide

An excerpt from Board Development materials.  This is an excellent (19-page) review of everything to do with creating and using a Board manual.

# Fundraising Resource Library Guide

Source: MAS Resource Library (SharePoint)

FUNDRAISING RESOURCE LIBRARY

Purpose

The purpose of the Fundraising Resource Library is to allow VCs to share tools and other resources. This can potentially save VCs considerable time and effort in developing original material when successful approaches already exist.

Accessing and Using Resource Library Material

The resource files are for use by any of the Fundraising VC’s. The ‘owner’ of the document is noted on each document – this is the VC that contributed the material.

Unless indicated otherwise, VCs can download and modify these files as required to satisfy their specific MAS client requirements.

The resource files themselves may be in the form of a presentation, tool, process, policy description/template or general information and advice on how to address a specific Fundraising topic.

VCs may contact the file owner directly if they have questions or wish to discuss the information in further detail.

Process for submitting and maintaining library material

To contribute resource material to the library VCs are requested to:

Ensure their resource file is in a user-friendly format with a brief description of the use of the material.

Email the file to Rita Daniel at rsdaniel@rogers.com who will arrange to have it posted in the Fundraising Resource Library.

Owners of resource files are encouraged to periodically review and update their material, as appropriate, using the above process. Any questions regarding the use of the Library should be directed to Rita Daniel at rsdaniel@rogers.com. Resource Library
